content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposes a network for learning shadow for 3D object generation. The proposed network optimizes for light location, latent vector which is used for object generation and the corresponding object pose jointly. The latent vector to be predicted is constrained by a pre-trained generative model so the network can always generate reasonable real-life objects.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
S:
Shadow can be used as a useful clue for predicting occluded objects in the scene. Though the idea is not so novel, it’s smart and interesting.

Introducing pre-trained generative model as a strong prior is a good way to enable the network to generate reasonable predictions stably.

Also, thanks to the pre-trained generative model, the proposed model can do joint estimation of lighting, object and its pose without the help of any other priors.

W:
Personally, I would not like to call the proposed method a reconstruction method since it uses only shadow information and it’s generating a set of solutions as the author indicated in the paper. Thus, a generative model may be more appropriate. 

The method relies heavily on the pre-trained generative model. And if the desired object is not included in the pre-trained model. The propose method may fails to give a proper or desired outputs.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Paper is well-written. 
Novelty: utilizing shadow for 3D-reconstruction is not new as the author stated. Applying pre-trained generative model for generation tasks is also not so novel as many works has already been exploited in NLP tasks. But joint estimation of lighting, object and pose from shadow under uncontrolled settings is quite new so I believe there are certain novelties with the proposed method.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall decent paper and I lean towards acceptance

content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper presents a method to reconstruct a 3D shape from a single image with shadow.
The proposed method trains a generative model by minimizing the error between the synthesized shadow and the shadow in the original image.
The shadow in this work is assumed to be a hard binary shadow.
The experiments of the synthesized dataset show the proposed method works well and can even recover the occluded objects.
The performance of natural scenes is also reasonable, but there is no example for occluded objects.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
++ The idea is straightforward and clearly described.

++ The performance of the synthesized dataset looks good. 

However, there are several concerns. 

-- The proposed method is firmly based on the binary shadow and can be segmented accurately. 
  There is no description of how to get the shadow in the synthesized dataset. Is it directly from known ground truth, or detected similarly a real scene?

-- If the shadow is soft, how will the result be?

-- How do the visual results of the comparative methods look like?

-- Where are the supplementary materials mentioned in Sec. 4.2?

-- There are no occlusion cases in the real-world dataset.

-- The ambiguity of the reconstructed 3D shape may restrict practical use. If multiple views can apply, how many views can eliminate ambiguity?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The clarity of the idea description is good, but some details of shadow detection are missing. 
The quality and novelty are fair.
The reproducibility is possible but may not be totally reproducing the results due to some implementation details in shadow detection and ambiguity in optimization.
The authors mention they will release the source code.
content.summary_of_the_review:
The paper presents an interesting solution for 3D shape reconstruction from shadow synthesis.
There are still many concerns to solve and the quality can be improved.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
•	The paper proposes a method to infer the shape of an object based on its shadow.
•	There are several assumptions, which are not explicitly stated in the paper: 1) there is only one light source, 2) the generator of the shape is provided, 3) the shadow can be accurately segmented, and 4) the shadow is cast on a plane.
•	The inference is to use a generator to generate parameters of the occupancy network to produce a shape.
•	The light source and the orientation of the object can be unknown.
•	The inference is based on optimizing the latent vector for generating the shape,  the light source direction (if unknown) and pose (if unknown).
•	The result of the optimization is the parameters for the occupancy network, which is trained for 4 different shapes, namely, car, chair, plane, and sofa.
•	The experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method can infer the shape of a shadow using only the shadow.
•	Compared with some baseline methods, the proposed method achieves better IoU.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
•	The paper is relatively easy to read and understand.
•	The results are quite interesting. 
•	Failure cases are also presented.
Weaknesses:
•	The main contribution is in the inference of the shape and not in the generation or representation of the object. While this is novel, the procedure is rather straightforward.
•	The assumptions of the method are not explicitly stated or discussed. For example, in a real environment, it would be uncommon to encounter a point light source or for that matter, a shadow with sharp boundaries. As well, to infer a shape in a practical application, from the description, the shape is assumed known a priori, which is not possible, in particular, when the actual object is occluded. Furthermore, the assumption that the shadow is on a flat surface would make such a method of limited use. As shown in the paper, an inaccurate segmentation of the shadow will create an object of a different shape. The above limitations are not discussed in the paper.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity:
The writing is clear and the paper is easy to follow. 
Originality and quality:
The problem appears to be a novel one. However, it may be a contrived problem because observing only the shadow without observing the object is not that common. Indeed, in the real world examples used in the paper, no objects are completely or partially occluded. It would be more interesting as well as more convincing if the authors could use some real world examples with the objects occluded completely. Another limitation is the requirement that the shadow is on a plane. Again, in many practical applications, e.g. the shadow of a cup on another cup, the surface is not a plane. In the related work section, there is no discussion of a recent work in ECCV 2022, titled, "DeepShadow: Neural Shape from Shadow."
content.summary_of_the_review: Shape from shadow is a long standing problem in computer vision. While using only the shadow to recover the shade is a novel problem, there is very limited examples to demonstrate what the method can do, in particular, real world examples. As well, the objects are required to be from a catalogue of shapes, which severely limits the use of the proposed method. What if the shape of the object is unknown? As far as I can tell from the paper, the proposed method would not be able to infer it. Finally, the proposed method is to apply optimization to find the best matched shape, which is rather straightforward. There is not much insight offered in the paper. In summary, the paper has not convinced me to accept the paper.

content.title: Shape Analysis by Shadow Synthesis
content.TL;DR: We propose a method to reconstruct a 3D object from just its shadow by inverting an implicit 3D generative model
content.abstract: 3D reconstruction is a fundamental problem in computer vision, and the task is especially challenging when the object to reconstruct is partially or fully occluded. We introduce a method that uses the shadows cast by an unobserved object in order to infer the possible 3D volumes under occlusion. We create a differentiable image formation model that allows us to jointly infer the 3D shape of an object, its pose, and the position of a light source. Since the approach is end-to-end differentiable, we are able to integrate learned priors of object geometry in order to generate realistic 3D shapes of different object categories. Experiments and visualizations show that the method is able to generate multiple possible solutions that are consistent with the observation of the shadow. Our approach works even when the position of the light source and object pose are both unknown. Our approach is also robust to real-world images where ground-truth shadow mask is unknown.
